idiom_name: generic free functions (Map/Filter/Reduce) and functions returning functions
implementation_notes: Go has first-class functions but no standard combinator vocabulary: with generics you write `func Map[T, U any](in []T, f func(T) U) []U` and the rest of the family yourself, and 'functions returning functions' (middleware, `func(Handler) Handler`) is idiomatic. The class hierarchy is replaced by these higher-order functions plus single-method interfaces. Third-party helpers such as samber/lo provide a lodash-style vocabulary when a team prefers a library to hand-written generics; concrete loops stay preferable in hot paths because each combiner allocates a result slice.
pitfalls: No currying: combiners take the whole slice, so a chain materialises an intermediate slice per step (and nil vs empty results differ under reflect.DeepEqual and JSON encoding).
Methods are not first-class values: you cannot pass `T.M` as `func(T)`, so wrapping in a closure is required and allocates on every step.
Methods cannot have type parameters, so generic combiners must be free functions or interfaces; error handling inside them is verbose without generics over error-carrying types.

variants.name: Go 1.23 iter.Seq push/pull iterators
variants.idiom_name: iter.Seq adaptors with range-over-func and the iter package
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23 makes `for range` accept iterator functions and ships the `iter` package (`type Seq[V any] func(yield func(V) bool)`), so a combinator library becomes lazy adaptor functions over `iter.Seq`, in the style of the standard `slices`/`maps` helpers (`slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted`, `maps.Keys`). Composition avoids intermediate slices entirely, and `iter.Pull` bridges to pull-style iteration. Choose it when pipelines are long or inputs large and the toolchain is at least Go 1.23.
pitfalls: Early exit depends on the yield result: a hand-written producer must stop when `yield` returns false or the range body's `break` leaks work (and the standard range loop does this for you).
A push iterator that starts goroutines or opens files must clean up on early exit, and any `iter.Pull` consumer must call the returned stop function or leak that cleanup.
Iterators are usually single-use in practice: documenting (and testing) re-iteration behaviour matters, because a second pass over a generated sequence repeats its side effects.
